event.description:
You've got your MCP connected but what's next? What does it take to turn an MCP connection into a working application?
Join speakers from Elastic, Arcade.dev, and Temporal for a developer meetup exploring three pieces of that puzzle: connecting agents to data, governing their access, and bringing tools together into workflows.
We’ll hear from:
Matt Ryan: Principal PM, Elastic — A look at Elastic’s new global MCP endpoint and what it enables for developers.
Evan Tahler: Head of Engineering, Arcade.dev — MCP governance: how to think about access and control as agents interact with your tools and systems.
Melanie Warrick: AI DevRel Engineer, Temporal.io — A multi-agent demo connecting Temporal and Elastic through the Temporal Agent Harness and MCP, showing how to control and manage a system of agents.
Together, these talks explore the practical questions behind building with MCP: What can your agents connect to? What should they be allowed to do? And how do those connections become part of a larger workflow?
If you’re building agents, developing MCP integrations, or figuring out how MCP fits into your stack, join us to explore the possibilities and meet other developers working through the same questions.
Bring your questions and the challenges you’re working on.
​🎟️ ElasticON SF
Join us Nov. 4 for a free day of hands-on learning, expert insights, and real-world AI, search, observability, and security sessions. Register for free.

event.description:
Join us for a fireside chat with David Rhew, Chief Medical Officer and VP of Healthcare at Microsoft.
The conversation will explore the rapidly evolving intersection of AI, healthcare, and AI for science. We’ll discuss how Artificial Intelligence is transforming healthcare delivery and clinical decision-making, and scientific innovation.
The session will bring together students, researchers, founders, investors, and industry leaders interested in the future of healthcare and AI.
About David Rhew:
Dr. David C. Rhew is the Global Chief Medical Officer (CMO) & VP of Healthcare for Microsoft. He is Adjunct Professor at Stanford University; holds six U.S. technology patents that enable authoring, mapping, and integration of clinical decision support into electronic health records; and has been recognized as one of the 50 most influential clinician executives by Modern Healthcare.
Dr. Rhew received his Bachelors of Science degrees in computer science and cellular molecular biology from University of Michigan. He received his MD degree from Northwestern University and completed internal medicine residency at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center. He completed fellowships in health services research at Cedars-Sinai and infectious diseases at the University of California, Los Angeles.
He has served as CMO and VP for Samsung; SVP and CMO at Zynx Health Incorporated; clinician/researcher at the VA Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System and RAND; and Associate Clinical Professor of Medicine at UCLA. Dr. Rhew has served on the National Quality Forum’s Executive Committee for Consensus Standards and Approval, Chaired the Consumer Technology Association Health Technology Board, and sits on the Governing Committee for NESTcc (National Evaluation System for health Technology coordinating center), the medical device advisory group for the FDA, CMS, and NIH.

Join this special ClawCamp Campfire to dive deeper into Sovereign AI, and owning more of your agentic AI Stack.
In a fast evolving agentic world where privacy is becoming harder and harder to maintain, and questions continue to rise around where your data goes and how it's being used by service providers; sovereign AI models, harnesses, and tools are evolving alongside their frontier counterparts. Join us to explore Sovereign AI options that allow you to own more of your agentic AI Stack, in order to maintain privacy and control access to your intellectual property.
This Campfire is hosted at the Luxor AI Cloud office, home of Tenki, and every attendee gets $500 in Tenki credits to run their own sandboxes (details below).
Learn more at ClawCamp.org
Want to Mentor, Speak, Sponsor, Volunteer, or Partner? Fill out our contact form: Aiify.io/form
📅 Schedule
6:00pm: Doors Open
6:30pm: Your Editor Local, Your Compute Anywhere: Crabbox + Tenki Sandboxes by Colin Lowenberg
6:45pm: Local AI Workshop by Jason Stine
7:40pm: Big Models, Little Machines: Distributed AI Workshop by Kirah Sapong
8:15pm: Scoping and Permissioning AI for a Shared Future by Rayyan Zahid
8:30pm: Networking and Wrap up
9:00pm: Doors Close
🎁 $500 in Tenki credits for every attendee
Tenki by Luxor.ai is sponsoring this Campfire with $500 in cloud credits per attendee, no credit card required.
Spend them on Sandboxes (Linux VMs your agent can run code in), GitHub Actions Runners, or Code Reviewer.
The fastest way in is to let your agent set itself up. Paste this into OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, or whichever harness you use:
Onboard me to Tenki. Follow the agent instructions at https://tenki.cloud/skill.md and set me up end to end.
📦 Your Editor Local, Your Compute Anywhere: Crabbox + Tenki Sandboxes by Colin Lowenberg
Running a model on your laptop keeps your prompts private. Running your agent's code on your laptop is a different problem: an agent that can run shell commands can also delete your home directory, and a laptop can only hold so many parallel jobs.
Crabbox (https://crabbox.sh), the new CLI from the OpenClaw team, solves this by keeping your editor and working tree local while running every command in the box you choose: a local container, your own SSH host, or a managed sandbox. Tenki is one of its providers, so the same crabbox run you use on your laptop can run on a fresh Linux VM in the cloud and stream the result back.
In 15 minutes, Colin will show:
crabbox run --provider tenki -- pnpm test from a local checkout, with the sandbox created, synced, run and torn down for you.
The OpenClaw Tenki sandbox backend (https://github.com/LuxorLabs/tenki-openclaw), so every tool call your OpenClaw agent makes runs in a remote VM instead of on your machine.
An OpenClaw gateway running entirely on a Tenki sandbox. Live demo at https://claw.moi
Worked examples to follow along with or try later:
Crabbox Tenki provider docs: https://crabbox.sh/providers/tenki.html
Crabbox + Tenki cookbook: https://github.com/LuxorLabs/cookbook/tree/main/examples/crabbox-tenki
OpenClaw Tenki plugin: https://github.com/LuxorLabs/tenki-openclaw
💻 Local AI Workshop by Jason Stine
Ever feel uncomfortable about sharing too much personal info with ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude but still want AI’s help? Against giving Big Tech your private life on a golden platter running on wasteful resource-sucking data centers? This workshop is for you! ​Earlier this year there was a breakthrough - we can now run AI that are more than capable of being private and even completely offline assistants on personal computers and laptops!
This is also a workshop for anyone who find setting up agents with OpenClaw too intimidating but still want a capable AI experience like ChatGPT that keeps all private information on their own computers - without writing any code or running any terminal/command line commands!
What we'll cover:
Setting up Unsloth Desktop (open source ChatGPT-like interface) and running powerful open source AI models of your choosing on your own computer.
Learning important concepts about running AI on your own computer - from why open source AI exists to tokens, context, model quantization, MCP tool servers, and more.
This is a hands-on workshop - bring your computer and get ready to download and install some AI!
System Requirements: The more RAM your computer has, the better. It’s now possible to run near-frontier-capable-AI on computers with just 16GB of RAM. That said, even if your computer has less than that (like 8GB), you can run less powerful AI that is still impressive and are welcome to attend!
To be efficient, we encourage participants to download and install Unsloth Desktop (https://unsloth.ai/docs/desktop) as well as let it automatically download a suitable AI model it selects for you (if any) when first running the app in advance before coming to the event. During the event, you’ll learn how to find even better AI models to add to your Unsloth Desktop setup.
🛠️Big Models, Little Machines: Distributed AI Workshop by Kirah Sapong
Running AI models on your own computer is exciting, but even powerful laptops have limits. By connecting multiple computers together, we can combine their resources to run larger AI models than any one device could handle alone.
In this workshop for all levels, we’ll explore distributed AI inference: how multiple computers can work together to run AI. We’ll demonstrate how to split AI models across devices using Aquaduck, without writing any code!
What we’ll cover:
Understanding how AI models run on your computer and why memory matters.
⁠Learning how multiple computers can work together to run AI.
Exploring model splitting and how it enables larger AI models to run across devices.
Getting hands-on with Aquaduck to connect computers and run AI together.
Bring your laptop and get ready to experiment with running AI across multiple devices.
You can download and install Aquaduck (https://aquaduck.ai) ahead of time so you can jump straight into the hands-on activities. No prior AI experience or programming knowledge is required.
✅ Scoping and Permissioning AI for a Shared Future by Rayyan Zahid
Rayyan will introduce some tips and strategies on properly setting the scopes and permissions for AI and agents.

🎤 Speakers & Mentors
Colin Lowenberg: Colin works on Tenki, the cloud sandbox platform from Luxor.ai, and runs Dabl Club, a builder community in San Francisco. He spends most days putting coding agents on remote VMs and keeping them off his laptop.
Jason Stine: Jason is actually in no way related to Unsloth. He's just a passionate AI hobbyist who enjoys mentoring others and found that Unsloth Desktop was the most straightforward software for this workshop. He's a fullstack web developer (software engineer) who uses Cursor AI every day at work.
Kirah Sapong: Kirah is a co-founder at Supermodel Labs, working on AI systems. Previously, she worked on model evaluations and AI platform products at Together AI, decentralized systems and developer platforms at Block, and is currently pursuing an M.S. in Artificial Intelligence at the University of Pennsylvania. Her research interests include agent systems, inference optimization, and AI economics.

I'm running my first-ever workshop at Hackaday Supercon this year. It's the "exquisite corpse" drawing game, but for electronics, and I'd love to do a trial run with friendly local faces first. Come be my workshop guinea pigs!
Here's how it will work: Everyone gets a small synth module and modifies it in secret. Then we chain all the blocks together, power them up, and find out whether our collective creation plays a tune you'll recognize. Exquisite Circuit: Exquisite Corpse for Electronics
What happens when a circuit is designed by a room full of people who cannot see the whole circuit?
In this hands-on electronic version of Exquisite Corpse, each participant adds a stage to a shared low-voltage circuit, conceals their work, and passes it to the next builder. Participants inherit standardized power and signal connections – but no schematic, explanation, or design review.
At the end, we reveal the complete creations, attempt to reconstruct their collective logic, inspect them for safety, and apply power from a strictly current-limited supply. Functionality is optional. Surprise is guaranteed.

Is Deployment the Real Moat in Physical AI?
What does it really take to deploy robots at scale, and can deployment become a lasting competitive advantage?
As robotics foundation models and hardware continue to advance, real-world deployment remains one of the industry's biggest challenges.
What separates a successful demo from a scalable business? Is the real moat in the technology, the deployment expertise, the operational data, or the customer relationships built along the way?
Join Embodied Collective for an intimate, curated industry conversation bringing together robotics companies, deployment practitioners, and enterprise adopters to exchange firsthand insights and explore what it takes to scale Physical AI in the real world.
What We'll Explore
The Deployment Bottleneck: What's actually preventing robots from scaling beyond pilots?
The Enterprise Perspective: What do industrial buyers really need before deploying robotics solutions?
Deployment as a Moat: Can real-world experience, data, and operational capabilities create sustainable competitive advantages?
Scaling in Practice: What does it take to make robotics deployments repeatable, reliable, and commercially viable?
Confirmed Speakers
Robert Scoble | Founder, Unaligned (Opening Fireside)
Robert has spent decades on the front lines of tech, from Microsoft to eight books about the future. He now tracks AI and robotics daily at Unaligned and AlignedNews.com, and visits the teams building them, giving him a rare view of what's actually running in the real world versus what's still a demo.
Ruslan Bekbulatov | Investment Principal, Bosch Ventures
Ruslan brings a unique perspective at the intersection of industrial customers and venture investing, engaging with both sides on technology capabilities, technical specifications, deployment timelines, and commercial considerations. (Views expressed are his own and do not represent Bosch or Bosch Ventures.)
Saman Farid | Founder & CEO, Formic
Saman runs Formic, which puts robots to work in American factories, and has an active and growing fleet deployed in 150 factories. In bringing Physical AI to the real world, his team has built infrastructure and software to handle deployment, monitoring and maintenance so manufacturers can automate without large upfront costs. Before Formic, he was a Partner at Baidu Ventures, leading investments in AI companies transforming traditional industries, and he founded Robots for America to advance U.S. robotics deployment policy.
Evan Tao | Co-founder & CEO, Chestnut Robotics
Formerly a core member of Tesla's Optimus team, Evan brings extensive robotics hardware experience from Tesla, Apple, and ASML. At Chestnut Robotics, he is advancing dexterous manipulation through hardware and human demonstration co-design, focusing on making robotic systems more reliable, scalable, and deployment-ready.
Natalia Kokoromyti | Co-founder & CEO, Cybernetic Physics
A Stanford computer scientist, Natalia previously worked as a researcher in Stanford’s Scaling Intelligence Lab, where she contributed to KernelBench, and worked on confidential computing at Lucid Computing. At Cybernetic Physics, an a16z speedrun company, she is building an intelligence lab for real-world machines. The company owns the hard part of putting robots to work, from bridging sim-to-real gaps and integrating robots on-site to policy serving, teleoperation, and ongoing operations, so autonomous systems can run reliably on real floors.
Judah Longgrear | Co-Founder and President of Media, Robot.com
Judah leads Robot.com's media business, R-Ads, building a first-of-its-kind robotic media network from the company's global fleet and digital out-of-home network. Robot.com is a Physical AI platform deploying autonomous robots across delivery, logistics, advertising, and security. A serial entrepreneur, Judah has spent nearly a decade building at the intersection of mobility, adtech, and robotics.
Rajesh Senthil Kumar | Head of Product and Deployment, RLWRLD
Rajesh leads product and deployment at RLWRLD, a Physical AI company developing RLDX-1, a dexterity-first robotics foundation model designed to enable human-like manipulation. By combining real-world industrial data with advanced robot learning, RLWRLD is tackling complex manipulation tasks across manufacturing, logistics, and service environments. Rajesh brings a practical perspective on bridging foundation model capabilities with real-world deployment and commercialization.

event.description:
Did Jesus Christ actually rise from the dead?
To most of us in the modern world, the question is almost so ridiculous that it's not even worth asking. Sure, Jesus may have had a few insightful moral teachings. It may even be the case that some find comfort and guidance from faith in Jesus. But to say that a 33 year old man from the backwaters of Galilee in the first century AD literally died, was buried, and miraculously came back to life is, at the very least, a bit ridiculous.
In this talk, Aditya Prathap will be making the case for why the resurrection of Jesus Christ is not only not ridiculous, but is in fact the only rational explanation of the objective historical data.
The talk will cover what is known as the Minimal Facts Argument. Concepts and sources that will be discussed include but are not limited to the following:
What Tacitus' comments on Christ in Annals (116 AD) tells us about the crucifixion of Christ.
What records of early Christian persecution from Suetonius (112 AD) and Pliny the Younger (121 AD) and the creed cited by the Apostle Paul in his letter to the Corinthians (54 AD) reveal about the sociopolitical landscape surrounding early Christians and its corresponding incentive structure.
Analysis of the medical literature relevant to common natural explanations of the historical data, including grief-induced hallucinations, mass hallucinations, and the symptoms of asphyxiation, the primary mechanism of death in Roman crucifixion.
Scholarly frameworks used to identify the reliability of data, e.g., the criterion of embarrassment.
People of any religious background or lack thereof are welcome to join. Skepticism and pushback are encouraged. No background in history or theology is needed. The talk will last ~45 minutes, followed by Q&A.
Aditya is a Christian living in San Francisco. Raised Hindu, he became an atheist after growing disillusioned with organized religion. After over a year of investigating the historical evidence for Christianity to prove that it had no rational justification, Aditya became convinced of the historicity of the resurrection of Jesus and was baptized in 2019.
event.title: The Historical Case for the Resurrection of Christ

Join us Tuesday, November 3rd at 5:30 PM for an evening with Stefanie Hutka, design leader and author of What Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation. Stefanie has spent her career asking a question that sounds simple until you try to answer it: what should automation actually do, and for whom?
Her talk centers on what she calls the "Automation Strategy Gap," the yawning distance between an organization's AI ambitions and its actual readiness to do something useful with them. It is, she argues, alarmingly wide. Drawing on human factors, cognitive science, and management theory, her book makes the case that AI is the latest chapter in a long history of automation, and that the durable lessons were always there, we just got distracted by the hype. One particularly useful provocation: automation accelerates the system you already have. Which means the first thing worth mapping is the beliefs driving your organization before you automate anything at all.
This is a book launch talk. Theme
This edition of Brain Gardeners’ Club explores how new forms of data and access can reshape what we know about the brain, and what clinicians can meaningfully do with it. There is currently a gap between the complexity of neurological disease and the required precision of care. Data’s value lies in its actionable therapeutic potential: helping clinicians understand where to go, what to sample, what to preserve, what to treat, and how to monitor disease over time.
The evening
We're bringing together builders and leaders at the forefront of neurotech, pharma and AI for an evening of candid conversation on the questions shaping the future of the brain: how new technologies reach patients, how data and AI change what’s possible, and what it takes to turn scientific progress into lasting impact.

Which gets built first, the power or the compute, and who signs for it.
When the first data center runs ninety days without a human inside, and what proof we will accept that it did.
Whether a handful of humans and a fleet of software agents can operate gigawatts, and what such a company must never be allowed to do. Where the waste heat of intelligence should go: into the air, or into greenhouses that feed a town.
Whether Europe builds its own or rents it.
